hook: The Pacific Ocean hit a record-shattering heat level months ahead of schedule.

sections.voiceover: The Pacific Ocean hit a record-shattering heat level months ahead of schedule.
sections.visual_cue: Satellite view of the Pacific Ocean with thermal mapping overlay.
b_roll: NASA Earth Observatory satellite imagery of Pacific sea surface temperatures

sections.voiceover: Did the Copernicus Climate Change Service record 29.70 degrees Celsius in that same Pacific region?
sections.visual_cue: Animated graph showing the 3.08 degree temperature anomaly spike.
b_roll: Data visualization of sea surface temperature anomalies

sections.voiceover: The Niño3.4 index, which tracks equatorial Pacific surface temperatures, surged to signal extreme climate shifts.
sections.visual_cue: Close-up of a digital weather monitoring interface showing the Niño3.4 index.
b_roll: Bureau of Meteorology climate monitoring dashboard

sections.voiceover: Australia's Bureau of Meteorology confirmed this index hit a record +2.88 degrees Celsius in October. This warming confirms a super El Niño, an intense climate pattern driven by Pacific heat.
sections.visual_cue: Bar chart showing the weekly record value of 2.88 degrees Celsius.
b_roll: Bar chart visualization of the Niño3.4 index record

sections.voiceover: That +2.88 degree index remains the highest recorded weekly value.
sections.visual_cue: Wide shot of the Pacific Ocean horizon at sunset.
b_roll: Cinematic wide shot of Pacific Ocean waves
